title: Utrecht implanted BCI gives a woman with locked-in ALS seven years of home communication
summary: A fully implanted ECoG interface turned band-power changes from attempted hand movement into clicks; she typed independently from 2016 and used it at home about seven years until ALS atrophy ended it.
account: Vansteensel et al. (NEJM, 12 November 2016) described a fully implanted brain-computer interface, subdural electrodes over the motor cortex with a subcutaneous transmitter, in a woman with late-stage ALS at UMC Utrecht: 28 weeks after electrode placement she controlled a typing program at about two letters per minute, used it outdoors where eye tracking failed as her only means of communication, and the authors note that suppressing unintended clicks 'required several months of refining the algorithms'. The 2024 NEJM follow-up reports seven years of independent at-home use, starting seven months after implantation; features from a single electrode pair (low- and high-frequency band power during attempted hand movement) were converted into click commands for spelling and a caregiver call; use declined close to six years after implantation as click accuracy fell, ended by March 2023, and the authors attribute this to ALS-related atrophy rather than device failure. Neither fetched text names a machine-learning decoder; the earlier verifier treated the decoder as threshold-based. The date is the 2016 publication date.
purpose: Provide autonomous communication for a person with late-stage ALS who could no longer rely on eye tracking
system: Fully implanted brain-computer interface: subdural electrodes over motor cortex, subcutaneous transmitter, click-based spelling (UMC Utrecht)
developer: University Medical Center Utrecht (Brain Center; Ramsey and Vansteensel)
deployer: University Medical Center Utrecht; home use by the participant
segment: People with locked-in syndrome from ALS
taxonomy_note: Kept under the no-discard rule although the AI/ML status is doubtful: the fetched texts describe conversion of band-power features into clicks with algorithms refined over months, and no classifier or learning method is named. The earlier verifier excluded it as threshold-based. Authors are the system's developers (academic), so the papers are marked vendor-authored.

ratings.reason: Sole means of communication outdoors and, over seven years, increasing at-home use as eye-gaze control was lost.

ai_role.statement: The interface's decoding is described as converting low- and high-frequency band-power changes from one electrode pair into click commands, with algorithms refined over months; no machine-learning decoder is named in the fetched texts, so whether this is an AI system in the database's sense is not established. The benefit itself (seven years of home communication) is documented in two peer-reviewed reports by the developers.
